review_text_raw:
SIMULACRA doesn't disappoint! I don't like to watch "Let's Play's" or anything before playing games because they tend to ruin some of the fun and that certainly is the case here. A lot of the complains I read from players is that they knew what was coming ahead of time... I had no idea and some of the things happening in my headphones genuinely terrified me because I legitimately thought they were happening in my house. I won't spoil what they were for anyone who has yet to play.

Still, like Sara is Missing, I think more can be done with this genre. The apps are fun to play with for a few minutes but it becomes apparent pretty quickly how shallow and underdeveloped they are. The dialogue is quite obviously written by someone to whom English is a second language and they didn't have anyone who speaks English proofread it. Lots of obvious typos and grammatical errors kind of took me out of the atmosphere. The voice acting by one of the characters is over the top to the point that it's cringey. The main character, though, is wonderfully acted and I couldn't tell at first that she wasn't actually American.

Overall I recommend this game to anyone into scares. Do yourself a favor and don't watch any gameplay footage because it will spoil a lot of the enjoyment.

[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

I found the game interesting and would have loved to see it through,but i couldn't bring myself to finish it.

In other reviews it's mention that it might be a bit of a slog to get through,but i found the information gathering,while repetitive to be quite nice and clever.

What stops me if the sudden jumpscars,they are not telegraphed well (there is very little to no indication that a jumpscared will happen,no tension build up,none of that,one moment you are looking through apps and suddenly you're struck with a jumpsacre when returning to the homepage).

As someone who is quite sensitive to jumpscares,even already knowing about the fact that there were jumpscares,the first major one was what stopped me from wanting to play.If the jumpscares were more subtle and less horrific i think it would have been more possible for me to finish,or at least get further in.

Another issue i had was that the game had no way of changing the volume inside the game,and i had to change it manually on my computer,someone who is less technically literate would probably have gotten an unintended jumpscare from the sudden volume from purely opening the game

The voice acting (with greg specifically) any many dialog was unrealistic,but i foudn it to be a more enjoyable part of the game,as they contrasted the poorly executed jumpscares in levity,though i would understand if it was not the intended effect.

it is truly a shame,because using the mediums and technology for this kind of horror would have been truly wonderful,clever and thought provoking,and even if nihilistic,the story  (as far as i have heard in other's videos and such) and how it applies it's title to it's themes could have been great.

i might look into it's sequals,but i may simply not have the stomach to actually go through on playing them,i hope you have a lovely day :D

Sad to say that I had to refund this. The premise seemed solid based on the store page - trying to piece together clues to someone's disappearance when you only have their phone - and the general interface was well done, but that was about it. My first hour of playing this mostly consisted of:

[list]
[*] Listening to overdramatic, very slowly worded voice messages.
[*] Piecing together "corrupted" pictures and texts that had absolutely nothing to do with Anna's disappearance. 
[*] Wondering if a proofreader was ever used for this game. Most of the articles and texts gave me the impression that English isn't the developer's first language. While I have nothing against that, coming across awkward grammar really took the immersion out of a mostly text-based game.
[*] Sitting through consecutive rounds of text-vomit finger-pointing from Greg and Taylor. I truly detest people who text at a rate of 50 messages/min when a single sentence would have sufficed. I didn't think it could get any worse, but in came the relationship drama...
[*] An overall disconnect between the gameplay and the plot. A girl disappears with clear hints of some non-human entity behind it, so why am I wasting my time investigating the sorry backgrounds of two garden-variety losers?
[/list]

Maybe the game gets better beyond the 1.7-hour point, but I really didn't have the patience to sit through constant notifications from the Male MC Idiot Express while waiting for some actual horror story to happen. Honestly, I'd have been happier to just shut the damn phone off and actually set out to find Anna door to door. At least then the "investigation" would have felt more productive.

review_text_raw:
The Good Stuff:

The layout and idea behind the game is pretty cool. I like how each "app" generally feels like a real app where you can do whatever, like comment of peoples posts or call random numbers. It is really neat design idea and it is well executed.

I also enjoyed a few of the more difficult puzzles, as they really added a sense of immersion into digging through someone's phone. The puzzles are mainly pretty easy, but the game doesn't baby you through them at all, so you feel smart when you manage to pull of something a bit more complicated.

The Bad Stuff:

For me, story is one of the most important parts of a game like this, and unfortunately SIMULACRA fails to deliver a good one.

Mild Spoilers: [spoiler]While the ending tried to be Black Mirror-esque, I feel like the story fails to properly set up the ending, so it kinda comes out of nowhere. Also, many things in the story aren't well explained or left to Deus Ex Machina[/spoiler]

There are multiple endings, and you will get an idea of what they all are when you finish the game. Some of the potential outcomes have me slightly curious, but not enough to replay it to see them. Perhaps the story would have been more interesting had I gotten a different ending.

I am not a huge fan of horror, but I have played games like Prey and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that have a creepy horror feel. The creepiness of SIMULACRA lasts only about the first 30 mins and then you become generally innoculated.

The main title song was also pretty cheesy.

[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

A lost phone appears in your grasp out of nowhere. When you peaked inside, you discovered a creepy video of someone else either asking for assistance or not. In this game, you are abruptly connected to unusual occurrences that put the people nearby in possibly deadly situations.


[H1] Visual: [/H1]
The UX and UI of this game are quite straightforward but interesting in their aesthetic design. Every "app" in this game has been designed in such a way that it is simple to grasp what it is and what kind of hint it is intended to give the player. A genuine smartphone design is featured in the game, along with a number of in-game applications modeled after well-known mobile applications including social media, apps, emails and other type of apps.

[H1] Audio [/H1]
Simulacra's original soundtrack will play during the main menu; it isn't very remarkable, but it wonderfully complements the game. The audio in this game is quite loud and intentionally intended to jump scare the player during the game's horror scenes. The voice acting of the actors aren't really good either. There is nothing else really interesting other than that.


[H1] Gameplay: [/H1]

Simulacra provides a decent horror experience. In this game, the choices you made along the way are tightly linked to one another. This game includes a memo so that you won't get lost if you forgot about the tasks you "need" to do. However, aside from the primary objective—which is to find Anna—they are not really a must-do. It is sometimes necessary to stop doing what you "should" do (based on memo) in order to achieve a different result (that would suit the player better). These messages may appear insignificant, but they contain information that the player will need later on. The difference in outcome will not be visible right away because they are sometimes piling on top of one another before reaching the turning point. The player would also need to uncover puzzles and collectibles throughout the game. In this game, finding those kinds of items is necessary in order to progress the story, unlike other games where they are optional. The puzzles are straightforward to solve; they consist of jumbled words, and all you need to do is choose the appropriate text to complete it. 


[spoiler] If you want to complete the game to the fullest extent possible, you will need to play it more than once because various accomplishments can be unlocked separately and you can only choose one of them. As the game has a few but game-breaking bugs, it would be more practical and less risky to just concentrate on one path at a time rather than reloading a backup save just to get all the achievements in a single run. Although it is possible to do it with the game saves and try to squeeze everything up in one playthrough. I suggest making backup files after chatting with Ashley about "who's at fault."

[/spoiler]


[H1] Controls [/H1]

Keyboard and Mouse are the only way to play it.

[H1] Pricing [/H1]

Worth the price

The voice acting is terrible and feels very performative, rather than being believable phone calls/voice messages. The story is linear, and there isn't much room for creativity (e.g. sending people random pictures to see how they respond), and there aren't really any things to mess around with on the phone that are interesting. The puzzles are ridiculously simple and serve no purpose other than to slow down the narrative. The jump scares, if you consider them that, are pretty pointless and don't enhance the story or experience whatsoever. The writing is generally bad and unbelievable (e.g. [spoiler]the CEO of Phresh Ideas divulging way too much information [/spoiler]), and many of the dialog options do not make sense at all. The characters frequently go between texting and calling in a way that doesn't feel believable, and behave very strangely (e.g. [spoiler]at the end of the game, a character is literally texting you as he's pushing someone to their death off of a balcony [/spoiler]). review_text_raw:
!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

This game is a bit annoying. I kinda enjoyed my time with it but it's just not good.

On the plus side: it's got decent social media puzzles and a sufficiently creepy atmosphere, ... and that's about all it has going for it. On the minus side: The writing is terrible, the voice acting is not great, there are several cheap jump scares, and the story itself is awful.

Ooh, the story has multiple endings and I should play again? No thank you, once is enough. I can't see what the game could have to offer besides more weak dialogue and weird railroady decisions.

Spoilers, I guess, but I lost and got the worst ending because I didn't show enough trust in the sleazebag (who was specifically written as a sleazy dude) ALL THE WAY IN THE BEGINNING OF THE GAME. It always bunches my britches when a game does that: "Oh you didn't do a thing when you didn't have all the information yet and you couldn't make an informed decision about it? Sucks to be you, Anna's dead." Oh, and also Taylor, he's dead too. Just because I wouldn't send the sleazy dude a cute selfie of the missing girl and I wasn't sufficiently sad enough about him being caught with his pants down (literally, fuck, it's such a contrived story).

I feel like the game is less about saving Anna and more about how you're supposed to protect the feelings of the two douchebag brodudes. There's only one other recurring character, Anna's best friend, Ashley, who could have been of great help, but the story sidelines her almost immediately and only brings her back to intimate that she's secretly in love with Anna. Again, spoilers, but if you've read this far, I doubt you care. (edit: Reading someone else's review, I just learned that to get the absolute best ending, you have to catfish the best friend and reciprocate her feelings without Anna's consent or Ashley's knowledge. Cool game, bro!)

Anyway, don't bother with this game unless you really want a 5 hour puzzle game with a crappy story.

review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

A story about an idiot surrounded by other idiots who sound like idiots.

At no point was there any reason to sympathize with Anna and her lifetime of bad decisions that got her into this mess. She's like the stereotypical white person in a horror movie whose phone suddenly goes to static and runs out of gas in the middle of the night in front of an obviously haunted house and says "I should investigate this immediately, and by myself!". Her dumbass ex, her dumbass new lover, her dumbass "best friend", all of whom supposedly want to help her yet they somehow form the main obstacles to doing so, especially the "best friend" who is basically a secondary antagonist for all the help she is. Aside from bit players like the completely unconvincing cop. I thought the cop was lying about being a cop and that that was important as first, but nope, just terrible voice acting, we're supposed to believe that's what cops sound like. Though he's not as bad as the villain revealed at the end, who sounds like a 13 year old boy who got his big brother to install voice changing software for him because he thinks it'll make him sound badass on voice chat while playing Halo. It's that bad. Was it supposed to be intimidating? Was it supposed to be a shocking reveal? It wasn't, just the annoying end to a nonsensical story about thoroughly unsympathetic idiots. I hope it at least has an "everyone dies" ending, because after meeting all of these characters, I honestly don't want any of them to live, it would be better for society for every one of them to go away.

[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

This was my first "found phone" type of mystery/horror to play so I was quite intrigued by the concept and mechanics as a whole. It really challenged how well of a snoop you were sometimes. Hilariously, I kept getting all the bad choices that ultimately led me to getting probably the worst ending possible and I wasn't really upset by that. However, there were some aspects that were a bit troubling for me throughout my playthrough. 

The jumpscares were considerably louder than the rest of the game and there are no audio options available. I guess I could understand if that was intentional since the "investigation" periods are very quiet (aside from [spoiler]the random knocks which were genuinely terrifying because I thought they were happening IRL[/spoiler]), but I actually did have fun just snooping through/messing with Anna's phone and texting everyone, so the cheap jumpscares took me out of the game pretty often.

Also, the climax (and the ending as a whole) just didn't totally sit right with me for some reason. Maybe my focus was waning by that point, but with hardly enough exposition to help drive the antagonist's motives, it just felt very out of left field. (Okay, maybe if I hadn't gone into this game ≈99% blind and maybe had also known [spoiler]what a simulacrum was[/spoiler], I would've had a better idea of what I was getting myself into.) With all that being said, I was left feeling underwhelmed and unsatisfied.

At the end of the day, SIMULACRA was [b]just okay[/b]. It's already very cheap in price, but I recommend you buy it during a sale if you're really that interested. I have just a small shred of hope for improvement on the second game.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10

[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]

I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world 
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.


On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. review_text_raw:
My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

review_text_raw:
Having played "A Normal Lost Phone", the concept of Simulacra isn't anything new to me, however due to this not being a particularly common way of making a game it is a welcome addition to this genre of sorts. 
Simulacra also comes with a couple of different twists compared to what "A Normal Lost Phone" had so it's not complete copy.

The good:
*You are thrown into an interesting story that you have to go through with the help of strangers. Who should you trust? Who should you be weary of? Wel that's the beauty, you don't know and you have to base your judgements on scraps of information that you can find. The story is definitely one of the highlights of this game.
*The gameplay whilst isn't groundbreaking works well for this game and doesn't propose any friction for the player on how to proceed.
*There's a decent bit of replayability in this game if you want to uncover all of the different paths. They also aren't particularly difficult to reach if given enough thought.

The bad:
*The horror elements of this game... Don't get me wrong, I love myself some horror and this game seems like a good candidate for a bit of it, however the way it is implemented in this specific game is forced and cliche.
Build tension through uneasiness, not through awful jumpscares.
*I don't need to be redirected to a webpage with a Discord server every time I finish the game. It is annoying. If I want to join your Discord Ill find a way to do it without it being showed in my face every time.
*For a game with so many branching I feel like it should've had a save system. If you want to get a specific achievement you are forced to replay the whole game. It is remedied by the faster conversations, but I do not want to listen to the same conversation for 7 times just so I can get an achievement.
*The acting leaves some things to be desired. I understand that this is an indie game but the video segments in this game felt somewhat robotic and lifeless.

Overall, Simulacra is a fun and interesting little game, that will not burn a hole in your wallet and will keep you entertained for a day or two. I think its worth giving a try, if you can stand the occasional jumpscare.

This is a tough call, especially given the price of the game. I'm going negative here because the "Overwhelmingly Positive" is out of line. This game is average, at best.

The concept itself is unique and the gameplay, for the most part, is well developed.

The main problem is the /r/nosleep storyline and unprofessional voice actors (especially Greg, I actually physically cringed when listening to his line deliveries). On top of that, there's some laughably blunt social commentary that's simply ridiculous. Someone else said it well, if they were going to be camp, they should have just gone all out campy horror. Instead, this is supposed to be serious and that's a shame.

Even more of a shame because the cryptology and detective stuff is really well done in this game. There's a lot of potential, and honestly, if you're that curious and can handle the bad acting and dumb direction the story takes, the measly 5% negative reviews aren't going to dissuade you from trying it out. 

But if you're on the fence, just look elsewhere.

For full transparency: I got this game in a Humble bundle worth 0.99 cents along with 1 other game.

[b][u]The good[/u][/b]
This game has an engaging story, I was seriously invested in the characters and how this was gonna play out. The characters really had a personality to them. The performance of the person playing Anna in particular was great! 
I liked the piecing together aspect this game had and how you slowly uncover more. It managed to hold my attention, for sure. It took me on a ride that I really enjoyed.
You can see that there was a lot of time and effort put into this game, with all the different things that are on the phone and all the conversations that play out. The little image and word puzzles were a nice touch, too. The game looks good and for the most part sounds good, too. 


[b][u]The bad[/u][/b]
The big reveal at the end of the game was… meh. The mystery to the game was much more fun than the answer to that mystery. Although I did like the endings themselves and their ambiguity.  
There were some repeated grammar mistakes that took me out of the experience. Yes, it’s texting, but I feel like in texting you get more typos and less grammar mistakes. The game would benefit from fixing some of these.
The voice acting was a bit spotty. Some actors did a good job, like the detective or Taylor. However, there was one audio clip of Ashley that felt immersion-breaking to me, and Greg in general didn’t sound good to me at all, it was way over the top.

[b]I encountered a game-breaking bug.[/b] For some reason, if you go in the web browser and go to the history section, all web pages that you should only be supposed to look at later in the game are already available. If you read these, events will trigger and the game will think you’re already at those points. The game then runs both the conversations you were already having and the “new” conversations which completely breaks your savefile. So, until this bug is fixed, [b]don’t look at anything in the history section of the web browser[/b].

[b]TL;DR Nice game, I definitely recommend it! But beware of the bug I talked about ^[/b]

The little image and word puzzles were a nice touch, too. The game looks good and for the most part sounds good, too. [b][u]The bad[/u][/b] The big reveal at the end of the game was… meh. The mystery to the game was much more fun than the answer to that mystery. Although I did like the endings themselves and their ambiguity. There were some repeated grammar mistakes that took me out of the experience. Yes, it’s texting, but I feel like in texting you get more typos and less grammar mistakes. The game would benefit from fixing some of these. The voice acting was a bit spotty. Some actors did a good job, like the detective or Taylor. However, there was one audio clip of Ashley that felt immersion-breaking to me, and Greg in general didn’t sound good to me at all, it was way over the top. [b]I encountered a game-breaking bug.[/b] For some reason, if you go in the web browser and go to the history section, all web pages that you should only be supposed to look at later in the game are already available. If you read these, events will trigger and the game will think you’re already at those points. The game then runs both the conversations you were already having and the “new” conversations which completely breaks your savefile. So, until this bug is fixed, [b]don’t look at anything in the history section of the web browser[/b]. [b]TL;DR Nice game, I definitely recommend it! But beware of the bug I talked about ^[/b]
